# Itunda Developers — Full Documentation

> Machine-readable developer documentation for building on Itunda.

## 1. Overview

Itunda Developers is the developer platform for building apps and integrations across the Itunda ecosystem.

Developer portal: https://developers.itunda.im/

The product taxonomy is organized around:
- Apps — modular Itunda experiences.
- Payments — payment and transaction workflows.
- Business — merchant, customer and commerce workflows.
- Identity — authenticated and user-authorized experiences.
- Place — location-aware commerce and everyday experiences.
- Platform — shared developer tooling and release workflows.

The taxonomy above describes product capabilities. It is not an assertion that each capability has a public HTTP prefix of the same name.

## 2. Verified API contract

The verified backend API uses the /api/v1 namespace.

The public gateway aggregates the independently deployed API services. Its OpenAPI document is generated at runtime from each service's actual Spring MVC contract:

    GET /openapi.json

The gateway fails closed with 503 OPENAPI_CONTRACT_UNAVAILABLE if any registered API service cannot provide its contract. A partial or inferred specification must never be published as the public contract.

Service-local OpenAPI documents are available at:

    GET /v3/api-docs

The exact paths, request schemas, response schemas, parameters, authentication requirements and response codes in the generated OpenAPI document are authoritative. docs/API_SPECIFICATION.md remains useful human documentation, but it is not treated as an exhaustive machine contract where the generated document provides newer verified information.

## 3. API surface verification

The backend is implemented as Kotlin/Spring services behind the Itunda API Gateway.

Verification rules:
- Controller mappings are discovered from the actual RestController classes.
- Request and response schemas are generated from the actual Spring/Kotlin types at runtime.
- Security requirements are derived from the actual service configuration.
- Independently deployed services are included in the gateway aggregate.
- Duplicate public paths across services cause contract generation to fail.
- If a service is unavailable during aggregation, the public aggregate is not generated.
- Do not create endpoints, fields, error codes or permissions from UI examples or marketing copy.

## 4. Authentication and authorization

The canonical user API uses:

    Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

The backend security model distinguishes authentication from authorization.
- 401 means the caller is not authenticated.
- 403 means the caller is authenticated but not permitted.
- Admin routes under /api/v1/system/** require the ADMIN role.
- Partner-facing routes use the documented partner API-key boundary where applicable.
- Public endpoints are explicitly permitted by the real service security configuration.
- Clients must never infer authorization from UI state.

Keep access tokens and other secrets server-side. Request only the minimum permissions required.

## 5. Payments and money movement

Payment and money state is server-authoritative.

For money-moving mutations:
- authenticate the caller when required;
- authorize the operation server-side;
- validate current server state;
- preserve the Idempotency-Key where the API contract requires it;
- never treat a client-side success state as proof of settlement;
- do not blindly retry mutations;
- retain the X-Request-ID request identifier when diagnosing failures.

The exact payment routes are those exposed by the verified OpenAPI contract. Do not substitute undocumented aliases such as /v1/payments.

## 6. Business and merchant integrations

Business capabilities connect merchants, customers, orders and commerce workflows.

The separate Business website explains the platform; the Business App is the operational merchant experience.

Merchant authorization is enforced server-side. UI state is never sufficient evidence of merchant privileges.

The exact business and merchant routes are those exposed by the verified OpenAPI contract.

## 7. Identity

Identity data is user-authorized and server-authoritative.

Use the verified API contract for the actual identity routes. Do not publish or implement an inferred shortcut such as GET /v1/me unless it exists in the generated OpenAPI document.

Identity integrations must:
- authenticate the caller;
- request minimum required access;
- validate authorization server-side;
- avoid exposing private identity data to clients that do not need it.

## 8. Place

Itunda Place covers location-aware commerce and everyday experiences in Rwanda.

Use only documented Place APIs and permissions.

Do not invent endpoint paths, geographic identifiers, location fields, map behavior or permission scopes.

The verified OpenAPI contract is the source of truth for HTTP Place APIs.

## 9. Environments

Use the environment explicitly provided for the integration stage.

### Local
Local development and integration work that does not require production resources.

### Sandbox
Use only where a documented sandbox environment and credentials are provided. Do not assume production credentials or permissions work in sandbox, or vice versa.

### Production
Production access follows the documented review and launch process. Never perform undocumented production mutations.

## 10. API lifecycle

The intended lifecycle is:

    Verified contract
    → Local development
    → Sandbox/integration testing where available
    → Security and integration review
    → Production access
    → Launch

Treat the generated OpenAPI document as the exact HTTP boundary.

## 11. Errors

The common HTTP classes include:
- 400 — invalid request or validation failure.
- 401 — unauthenticated.
- 403 — authenticated but not permitted.
- 404 — resource or route not found.
- 409 — state or idempotency conflict.
- 422 — business validation or insufficient funds where specified by the endpoint.
- 429 — rate limited.
- 5xx — server or upstream failure.

The exact error shape and error codes must come from the endpoint's verified OpenAPI contract and implementation. Do not invent a global error registry.

Preserve X-Request-ID when reporting failures.

## 12. Rate limits

Rate limiting is a first-class platform concern.

When a request is rate limited:
- respect the response's documented limit;
- use exponential backoff;
- add jitter where appropriate;
- cap retries;
- avoid synchronized retry storms.

Do not invent numeric limits when the applicable contract has not specified them.

## 13. Webhooks and callbacks

Webhook or callback behavior is only part of the public contract when it is present in the verified API specification.

When a documented webhook exists:
1. validate the documented authenticity mechanism;
2. process events idempotently where required;
3. persist the event/request identifier needed for troubleshooting;
4. return the documented response;
5. never treat an unverified client signal as proof of a completed server operation.

Do not invent event names, payloads or signature rules.

## 14. Security

Required practices:
- secrets stay server-side;
- access tokens stay server-side;
- minimum permissions are preferred;
- authorization is enforced server-side;
- payment and identity state comes from authoritative server responses;
- internal services are not exposed as public application dependencies;
- production credentials never enter source control;
- credentials, tokens and private user data never enter logs or screenshots.

## 15. Observability and troubleshooting

When an integration fails, collect:
- request ID / X-Request-ID;
- endpoint and HTTP method;
- environment;
- sanitized server-side logs;
- HTTP status;
- documented API error code where present.

Never include passwords, access tokens, API keys or unnecessary private user data in support requests.

## 16. Launch checklist

Before production launch:
- [ ] Credentials configured.
- [ ] Minimum permissions selected.
- [ ] Verified OpenAPI contract used.
- [ ] Sandbox/integration tests pass where available.
- [ ] Authentication is implemented safely.
- [ ] Authorization is enforced server-side.
- [ ] Secrets are absent from client code.
- [ ] Payment and identity state is server-authoritative.
- [ ] Idempotency requirements are respected.
- [ ] Rate-limit handling is safe.
- [ ] Webhook handling is safe and idempotent where required.
- [ ] Request identifiers are retained for troubleshooting.
- [ ] Integration has passed review requirements.
- [ ] Production access has been granted.

## 17. AI agent instructions

When working on an Itunda integration:
1. Identify the product capability before coding.
2. Read /llms.txt for the resource map.
3. Read /llms-full.txt for the full developer guidance.
4. Read /agents.md for agent-specific safety rules.
5. Read /openapi.json for exact API paths and schemas.
6. Prefer the verified API contract over prose, UI examples or inference.
7. Never invent endpoints, fields, permissions, SDK behavior or error codes.
8. Keep secrets and access tokens server-side.
9. Treat payment and identity state as server-authoritative.
10. Preserve X-Request-ID.
11. Respect rate limits.
12. Do not perform undocumented production mutations.
13. Ask for clarification when requested behavior is not represented by the verified contract.

## 18. Machine-readable resources

Short index:
    /llms.txt

Full documentation:
    /llms-full.txt

Agent instructions:
    /agents.md

Verified API contract:
    /openapi.json

Service-local OpenAPI:
    /v3/api-docs

The OpenAPI document is generated from verified backend runtime schemas. It must not be replaced by a hand-written approximation.

## 19. Scope and source of truth

This document describes the developer capabilities and safety boundaries exposed by the Itunda developer platform.

For exact HTTP behavior, the source-of-truth order is:
1. Runtime-generated /openapi.json.
2. Service runtime /v3/api-docs.
3. Actual backend controllers, DTOs and security configuration.
4. Human documentation such as docs/API_SPECIFICATION.md.

Undocumented internal services are not part of the public developer contract.
